Lateral epicondylitis is highly plausible given the classic distribution (lateral elbow → dorsal thumb/wrist) and chronicity; although the provocative test wasn’t performed, its absence doesn’t exclude it. Cervical radiculopathy (C6–C7) fits the dermatomal/myotomal spread (thumb, wrist extensors, lateral forearm, elbow) and chronic insidious onset — especially if symptoms are positional or associated with neck stiffness. De Quervain tenosynovitis explains thumb/wrist pain but less commonly refers *up* to the elbow; however, chronic cases can involve compensatory biomechanics or perceived radiation. Radial tunnel syndrome is a less common but distinct mimic: it causes deep lateral elbow/forearm pain with possible thumb/wrist involvement and no objective nerve conduction abnormality, often misdiagnosed as epicondylitis. Carpal tunnel syndrome is lower confidence because it typically spares the elbow and lateral forearm, and pain rarely radiates proximally beyond the wrist — though severe or longstanding cases may report referred discomfort; however, classic presentation is nocturnal paresthesias in median-innervated digits (thumb–index–middle), not isolated thumb/wrist pain radiating upward."}
